---
title: "Earlier-versus-later Helmert contrasts"
---

The [Helmert-coding page](helmert-coding.qmd) constructed a sequence in which each later level was compared
with the average of earlier levels. We can reverse the grouping question. At
each step, compare an earlier level with the average of the levels that follow
it.

This contrast family is usually called [**reverse Helmert contrasts**](https://stat.ethz.ch/R-manual/R-devel/library/stats/html/contrast.html). Some sources use *inverse Helmert contrasts*. The displayed matrix, rather than the label alone, determines the interpretation.

Suppose a stress factor has three ordered levels: primary stress, secondary
stress, and unstressed. A phonetic hypothesis might compare primary stress with
the average of the two weaker categories, then compare secondary stress with
unstressed.

One unscaled reverse Helmert matrix is

$$
\begin{array}{c|rr}
&C_1&C_2\\\hline
\text{primary}&2&0\\
\text{secondary}&-1&1\\
\text{unstressed}&-1&-1
\end{array}.
$$

The first column compares primary stress with the average of secondary and
unstressed. The second compares secondary stress with unstressed.

## Deriving the coefficient meanings

The linear predictor is

$$
\eta_i=\beta_0+\beta_1C_{1i}+\beta_2C_{2i}.
$$

Substituting each row gives

$$
\eta_{\text{primary}}=\beta_0+2\beta_1,
$$

$$
\eta_{\text{secondary}}=\beta_0-\beta_1+\beta_2,
$$

and

$$
\eta_{\text{unstressed}}=\beta_0-\beta_1-\beta_2.
$$

The primary-minus-weaker-average comparison is

$$
\begin{aligned}
\eta_{\text{primary}}
-\frac{\eta_{\text{secondary}}+\eta_{\text{unstressed}}}{2}
&=(\beta_0+2\beta_1)-(\beta_0-\beta_1)\\
&=3\beta_1.
\end{aligned}
$$

The secondary-minus-unstressed comparison is

$$
\eta_{\text{secondary}}-\eta_{\text{unstressed}}=2\beta_2.
$$

The coefficients encode the reverse Helmert comparisons after accounting for column scaling. Dividing
the first column by 3 and the second by 2 would make each coefficient equal the
corresponding raw mean difference.

## When the comparisons are meaningful

ELCs are useful when a theory distinguishes one leading category from a set of
categories ordered below it. For the stress example, the first hypothesis groups
secondary and unstressed as weaker than primary stress. The second asks whether
the two weaker categories are themselves different.

This interpretation requires more than a meaningful order. It requires the
particular nested groupings encoded by the columns. Applying reverse Helmert contrasts to an unordered
set of dialects would create arbitrary comparisons. Applying them to an ordered
factor is also unmotivated if the theory asks for different groupings.

Ordering alone does not justify reverse Helmert contrasts. Order makes the comparison sequence possible. It does not make
that sequence theoretically relevant.

## Inspecting predictions as a check

No full-rank contrast matrix changes the fitted mean for each factor level when
the same complete model is used. After fitting, reconstruct the level means and
verify that the coefficient interpretation matches the matrix.

```{r}
#| label: construct-earlier-versus-later-contrasts
#| echo: true
stress_data <- data.frame(
  stress = factor(
    c("primary", "secondary", "unstressed"),
    levels = c("primary", "secondary", "unstressed")
  )
)

elc <- matrix(
  c(2, -1, -1,
    0,  1, -1),
  nrow = 3,
  ncol = 2
)

colnames(elc) <- c("primary_vs_weaker", "secondary_vs_unstressed")
rownames(elc) <- levels(stress_data$stress)

contrasts(stress_data$stress) <- elc
contrasts(stress_data$stress)
```

Constructing the matrix explicitly makes the sign and grouping visible. A
package function may use the opposite sign, a different scaling, or the opposite
naming convention. Do not infer the coefficient meaning from a function name
alone.

## Reconstructing a numerical example

Suppose the fitted duration means are 120 milliseconds for primary stress, 92
for secondary stress, and 76 for unstressed syllables. The first reverse Helmert comparison is

$$
120-\frac{92+76}{2}=36.
$$

Under the unscaled matrix,

$$
\beta_1=\frac{36}{3}=12.
$$

The second reverse Helmert comparison is

$$
92-76=16,
$$

so

$$
\beta_2=\frac{16}{2}=8.
$$

The intercept is the unweighted average of the three means:

$$
\beta_0=\frac{120+92+76}{3}=96.
$$

Substituting $(\beta_0,\beta_1,\beta_2)=(96,12,8)$ into the three design rows
recovers 120, 92, and 76.

## Keeping sign and grouping separate

Multiplying an entire contrast column by $-1$ reverses the sign of its
coefficient. The fitted category means remain unchanged. Reordering factor
levels, in contrast, can change which categories are grouped together. These are
different operations.

For this reason, state the comparison in words and provide the
matrix. "We used reverse Helmert contrasts" is not enough when the terminology and
sign convention can vary.

::: {.callout-note title="Recover the reverse Helmert coefficients"}
1. What does the second reverse Helmert contrast compare in the displayed three-level factor?
2. Why is the primary-minus-weaker-average difference equal to $3\beta_1$?
3. Verify the three fitted means using $(96,12,8)$.
4. Explain why an ordered factor does not by itself justify reverse Helmert contrasts.
5. Why should a report provide the matrix in addition to a contrast-family name?
:::
